lines.note: The opening gado completes the preceding page's carregado. Tsurakuse ga warui hito describes a person with an unpleasant or gloomy habitual expression; Ho- begins the Portuguese homem.
Completes homem and describes an ill-favoured, melancholy countenance. The older Portuguese malenconizado is retained rather than replaced with a modern adjective.

runs.text: naturalmente, ou que por algũà cauſa eſtà car-

lines.note: The gloom may be natural or caused by some circumstance. The printed marks in algũà and eſtà are retained; car- continues the adjective carregado below.
Completes carregado, describing the burdened or clouded expression. The short continuation closes the preceding example before the new headword.

runs.text: Homem que no geſto, ou ſem-

lines.note: Tsuradamashii describes someone whose expression reveals an inward disposition. The scan reads Tçuradamaxij, not OCR Tçutadamaxij; Japanese x corresponds to sh here.

runs.text: brante moſtra algum affeito interior como de

lines.note: The countenance displays some inward affection or emotion. Portuguese affeito is the printed historical form and the examples of such feeling follow below.
Anger and severity exemplify the inward feelings visible in the face. This row completes the definition of Tçuradamaxij.

The headword denotes the jaw or facial outline, identified as tsuragamachi by the example below and NINJAL 250a02. The expected c position is nearly blank in this impression; retain the visible Tçuragama hi rather than silently filling the damaged gap.
Tsuragamachi no yoi or warui hito describes a person whose face or jaw is good-looking or ill-looking. Latin l introduces the alternative; the example continues from the preceding Tçuraga-.

runs.text: ou mal parecido das faces, & queixadas.

lines.note: Completes the comparison: good or bad appearance of the cheeks and jaws. The Portuguese ties this entry specifically to the facial outline.
Tsurai is introduced as an expression of complaint. The following gloss explains the painful or unkind quality being complained of.

runs.text: couſa deshumana, ou pouco apraziuel, & ſem

lines.note: The quality is inhuman, unpleasing, and without pity. The scan supports deshumana with a short s and apraziuel in place of OCR dechumana and apraziael; historical spelling is retained.
Completes sem piedade and adds that the action strikes the heart. This expresses the emotional hurt associated with tsurai.
Tçuraſa is the nominal form, tsurasa, of the preceding adjective: its harshness, cruelty, or painfulness. No Portuguese gloss is printed on this short derivative row.
Tçurǒ is the contracted adverbial form corresponding to tsuraku. The downward caron is retained as printed, without inserting an additional explanatory vowel.
Tsuranari means being strung together or arranged in sequence. The scan supports Tçuranari and enfiada across this and the next row; the abbreviated principal part u is retained as printed.
Completes enfiada and adds being placed in order. Za ni tsuranaru illustrates taking one's place in an ordered seated assembly.

runs.text: Eſtar no Zaxi qui por ordem. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese explains occupying a place in the zashiki in order. The Japanese room-name is abraded and is retained as Zaxi qui with a visible gap; Ichimon- begins the next example about family affiliation.
Ichimon ni tsuranaru hito means a person belonging to or related to a family. The printed joined nitçuranaru continues Ichimon- from the preceding row.

runs.text: algũa familia, ou que he daqu lla gèração, &

lines.note: The person belongs to a particular family or lineage. The e position in daqu lla is nearly blank; the OCR's visible gap is retained rather than silently supplying daquella, whose meaning the context establishes.
Linhagem completes the Portuguese account of family descent. The short row belongs to tsuranari, before the transitive verb tsurane.
Tsurane is the transitive counterpart: stringing things or putting them in order. The principal form is uru, and the Portuguese reads Enfiar; por por ordem is retained as printed.
Uta wo tsuranuru illustrates arranging or composing verses. The example has tçuranuru, with the faint middle vowel resolved against the visible repeated tsurane forms; Com- continues below.

Completes Compor versos. Shugyoku wo tsuranetaru begins the example about strung precious stones; the abraded Xuguiocuuo is chosen from the surviving types and the jewellery gloss, with the uncertainty retained.

runs.text: Veſtido ornado com pedras precioſas ẽ-

lines.note: Ishoo completes the Japanese phrase for a garment adorned with strung jewels. The caron in ixǒ and the abbreviation tilde in the divided Portuguese ẽ-fiadas are retained.
Fiadas completes enfiadas, specifying that the precious stones decorating the garment are strung together. This closes the tsurane example.

runs.text: Certo calçado de couro duro q̃ ſer-

lines.note: The noun tsuranuki names a kind of stiff leather footwear. The scan's q̃ is an unexpanded abbreviation for Portuguese que, and ſer- continues below.
The footwear serves for hunting or warfare. The printed joined naguerra is retained and this row closes the footwear entry.
The verb tsuranuki means threading or piercing. Its a is almost uninked in the headword; retain the scan's Tçur. nuqi with a caveat, while the full example below identifies the intended verb.
Tama wo tsuranuku illustrates threading precious stones. The Portuguese translation begins En- and is completed on the following row.

runs.text: fiar pedras precioſas em algum cordão, ou nou-

lines.note: Completes enfiar: stringing precious stones onto a cord or something else. Precioſas retains the visible long s, correcting OCR preciolas; nou- continues noutra.
Completes noutra cousa. Yari ni tsuranukarete shinu- begins an example of being pierced by a spear and dying; the verb's ending follows below.
Ru completes shinuru, to die. The Portuguese gives dying from a lance thrust or being pierced; atraueſado is retained without supplying a second s.
Algũa lança completes the instrument of the fatal piercing. This short continuation closes the verb tsuranuku.

runs.text: Candeas do caramelo que fica depen-

lines.note: Tsurara denotes icicles, described as candles of ice. Historical Portuguese caramelo here means frozen ice, as the hanging-from-eaves explanation makes clear; it is not a sweet confection.
The icicles hang from the edges of the roof. This completes the concrete comparison introduced by candeas do caramelo.
Tsuratsura is marked as an adverb and glossed attentively. The following Tçu- begins the example that continues on the next physical row.
Tsuratsura anzuru means considering something attentively. The final a- begins Portuguese atentamente, whose remaining syllables occupy the next row.
Completes atentamente, closing the example of careful consideration. The physical continuation indentation is restored from the scan.
Tsure is first explained by rui, a kind or class, and Portuguese laya. Sono tsure no begins the example for something of that kind; the worn Rui is retained.
Mono completes sono tsure no mono, a thing of that kind. Portuguese cousa deßa laya gives the same meaning, and the continuation indentation is restored.
The second tsure means company or a group of companions. Rokuninzzure begins an example of a company numbering six; the printed doubled z is retained.
The six-person-company gloss is completed, then a new example begins Foogan do-. The title and honorific continue as dono on the next row; the caron in Fǒguan is retained.
Dono no on tsure denotes the lord or official's company or companion. The beginning completes do-nono, correcting OCR neno; companhei continues into ro without an invented terminal hyphen.

Completes companheiro de Fóguandono, the companion of the person styled Foogan-dono. The o is partly erased and only an acute-shaped stroke survives above it; a damaged caron cannot be excluded, so the caron from c1-l043 is not silently copied here.
Tsure as a verb means taking someone along in company. The divided Portuguese compa- continues on the next row, while uru and eta retain the printed principal-part notation.
Completes companhia. Kaze ni tsureraruru describes being carried by the wind; the scan reads nhia and leua-, correcting OCR phia and leu, with leua-do continuing at the head of column 2.
Do completes leua-do from the foot of column 1: being carried by the wind. Hito wo tsururu introduces taking a person along; Co- begins the following usage explanation.

runs.text: mummente ſe vſa com eſta voz,

lines.note: Completes Comummente, explaining that tsururu is commonly used with the prefixed verb mexi. Mexi is a Japanese term inside Portuguese commentary and is retained in roman type; Vt is italic.
Meshitsururu means taking someone along in one's company. The Portuguese statement continues below with a restriction on the social relation involved.

runs.text: mas não ſe dirà de gente mais alta, ou igual.

lines.note: The construction is not applied to someone of higher or equal standing. This is the dictionary's register restriction, completing the usage note above.

Ko or komono wo meshitsureoozu is an intention to take one's children or attendants along. The initial paragraph sign is restored, and the scan's clear circumflex in mexitçureôzu is preserved instead of the OCR caron.

runs.text: Leuarei comigo os filhos, ou moç s.

lines.note: The Portuguese says 'I shall take the children or lads with me'; Leuarei corrects OCR Leuares. In moç s the second o is almost uninked, so the visible gap is retained with the lexical interpretation made explicit.
Tsuredachi means going or taking someone in company. The principal parts preserve tçu and atta, while Portuguese cõ- continues companhia with its printed abbreviation tilde.

The example describes two people accompanying one another. The scan reads Fucari, though the bilingual context calls for futari; the c-like type lacks a clear t ascender and is retained as a printed anomaly. Vo- continues below.
Giare completes the respectful request form vo-giare. The citation label Mon. precedes the Portuguese 'bring both with you' and remains roman rather than part of the italic translation.
Tsuurei means an ordinary custom, explained by tsune no katagi. The scan supplies the missing ç and a downward caron in Tçǔrei, correcting the OCR's broken T,ǔrei.
Dinario completes ordinario, the ordinary or customary practice gloss. This short continuation belongs to tsuurei.

runs.text: Romance que cantão dous, ou mais

lines.note: Tsuremai is first a song or ballad performed by two or more people. Romance is the Portuguese performance term here, not a claim about a modern romantic narrative.

runs.text: juntos. ¶ Item, Bailo que fazem dous, ou

lines.note: Juntos completes the joint-singing definition. The second meaning is a dance performed by two or more people, with further details below.

runs.text: mais de companhia com os abanos, como ſe faz

lines.note: The dancers perform together using fans. The Portuguese abanos denotes the fans employed in the shared dance, and the comparison continues below.
The performance is compared with what is done in plays or dramatic pieces. Autos supplies that theatrical context and closes the tsuremai entry.
Tsurenai is explained by omote katashi, having a hard face or manner. Portuguese dura begins the explanation of hardness or unfeeling severity.
The gloss adds lack of pity and severity. Tçurenai fi- begins the example of such a person; the damaged initial T is restored without the OCR's spurious internal space.

runs.text: Homem, ou peßoa que mostra pouca pie-

lines.note: To completes hito, a person. The Portuguese describes someone showing little pity; the provisional short-s spelling mostra is retained in this difficult italic st class.

runs.text: dade, ou duro, & ſeuero em conceder algũa cou-

lines.note: The person is hard or severe in granting something. The final cou- continues cousa; the Portuguese wording links this severity with refusing or restricting a request.
Completes cousa, then gives tsurenai inochi: a life so long that its length is burdensome. Com- begins the adjective comprida on the following row.

runs.text: prida que jà di pena, & moleſtia.

lines.note: Completes comprida: the life is so long that it causes pain and distress. The scan retains the narrow i-like form in jà di pena; the context calls for dà/dá pena, but no secure a bowl survives, so di is preserved with this caveat.
Tçurenaſa is the nominal derivative tsurenasa, referring to the preceding quality of unfeeling hardness. It occupies its own short indented physical row.

Tçurenǒ is the contracted adverbial form; hito ni tsurenoo ataru illustrates behaving harshly toward someone. Only the paragraph sign between the derivative and example is printed, so the OCR's initial sign is removed.
The Portuguese explains cruelly striking or hurting someone's heart. This completes the harsh-treatment example rather than introducing another headword.
Tsurekitari means bringing someone along while coming. The Portuguese vindo trazer expresses that direction of movement, and alguẽ retains its abbreviation tilde.
Consigo completes the explanation of coming with someone in one's company. This short row closes tsurekitari.
Tsurezure and tsurezurena are explained by tozenna, lonely or solitary. The two z letters in each form and the doubled n in Tojenna are retained as printed.
The Portuguese gloss is a solitary condition or thing. It closes the tsurezure entry, without adding later senses such as writing miscellanies.

Tsuri is here a fishing hook. The example visibly reads Tçurino taruru with n, although its Portuguese gloss means fishing with a hook; retain the anomalous particle spelling rather than silently changing it to uo.
Completes pescar com anzol. Tsuri wo suru gives another way to say fishing, explicitly equated by Idem; its clear u contrasts with the preceding example's n.
Tsuri as a verb means fishing. Io wo tsu- begins the example 'catch fish'; the printed Iuo is retained rather than modernized to uo.
Ru completes tsuru. A second sense is hanging something up, followed by the example on the next physical row.
Kaya wo tsuru means setting up or suspending a mosquito net. The Portuguese armar ou dependurar begins the translation, and its article continues into Caya below.
Caya completes the Portuguese reference to the mosquito net and is marked as an embedded Japanese term. A further tsuri sense means contracting or shrinking.
The contraction is compared with a nerve or sinew tightening. Sujiga begins suji ga tsuru; the historical gi spelling is retained in the example.
Tsuru completes the example of a sinew contracting. The final sense means becoming irritated; its abbreviated principal part u is retained as printed.
Tsuriage means hanging or lifting something up. The Portuguese reads Dependurar, correcting the OCR vowel in Dependarar, and the height specification continues below.
Em alto completes the meaning 'up high'. This is a short continuation of tsuriage, not another hanging-related entry.
Tsuribari is explicitly a fishhook. The brief Portuguese anzol matches the compound formed from fishing and needle or hook.
Tsuribito is a person who fishes with a rod. The d of Peſcador is worn, but the surviving ascender and the rod-fishing gloss support it over OCR Peſcaor.
The first tsuribune is a fishing vessel. The gloss also allows a boat from which hook-and-line fishing is done, completed below.
Fishing with a hook completes the first tsuribune explanation. Its physical continuation indent is restored from the scan.

runs.text: Vaſo à maneira de naueta de pen-

lines.note: The second tsuribune is a hanging, boat-shaped vessel. This distinct entry begins the historical description of a suspended flower container; the weak de after naueta is retained.

runs.text: durada q̃ antiguamente ſeruia de porem flores,

lines.note: The hanging container formerly held flowers. The scan reads antiguamente rather than OCR amiguamente, retaining the source's older form and unexpanded q̃.
Leaves could also be placed in the container. Fullas is the printed form and is not modernized to folhas; nella supplies the vowel missed by OCR nlla.
Tsuridana is a shelf suspended or fixed high up. The printed Parteleiro is retained rather than regularized to modern prateleiro; pre- begins pregado below.
Gado completes pregado, fixed or nailed in a high position. This closes the final body entry; the isolated Tçuri- below is page furniture and is not appended to this line.
The ç is faint; Tçuri- is the chosen reading of this isolated lower-right catchword, and the fragment is not part of the final body definition.
